clinicalPearls: Characterised by intense, cramping or spasm-like pain in the parotid region with the first bite or chew of each meal, easing markedly over the next few mouthfuls
The pain is worst at the start of eating, provoked most strongly by sour or tart foods, and recurs at the next meal
Typically follows surgery in the parapharyngeal space, deep lobe parotid, or upper neck that disturbs cervical sympathetic supply to the parotid
It may also be the presenting feature of a parapharyngeal space tumour, so new spontaneous first bite pain warrants imaging
The mechanism is loss of sympathetic tone to parotid myoepithelial cells with unopposed parasympathetic supersensitivity, causing painful contraction with initial salivary stimulation
Botulinum toxin injected into the parotid gland is the most effective treatment for refractory cases; carbamazepine and other neuropathic agents give variable benefit
Symptoms often improve gradually over months as the nervous system adapts
reference.pathophysiology: First bite syndrome is attributed to loss of sympathetic innervation to the parotid gland, usually after surgery involving the parapharyngeal space or cervical sympathetic chain. Denervation leaves the parasympathetic supply to the myoepithelial cells relatively unopposed, and these cells become supersensitive. The strong burst of parasympathetic (salivary) stimulation at the first bite of a meal then provokes an exaggerated, painful contraction of the myoepithelial cells. As salivation continues over subsequent bites the stimulus diminishes and the pain subsides, giving the characteristic pattern that repeats at the next meal.
additionalDifferentials: Salivary duct calculus with mealtime pain
additionalInvestigations: Detailed history establishing the classic first-bite, sour-food-provoked pattern
Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the parapharyngeal space and deep parotid to exclude a mass
Ultrasound of the salivary glands to exclude obstruction or sialadenitis
Review of prior operative records for parapharyngeal or sympathetic chain surgery
Sialography or salivary duct assessment if obstruction is suspected
redFlags: New spontaneous first bite pain without prior surgery, suggesting an occult parapharyngeal tumour
An associated Horner syndrome indicating sympathetic chain involvement by disease
A palpable deep neck or parapharyngeal mass
Progressive cranial neuropathies accompanying the pain
reference.prognosis: The syndrome is benign and tends to lessen in intensity over months to a couple of years, though it may persist. Botulinum toxin provides reliable temporary relief and can be repeated; spontaneous first bite pain resolves once any underlying tumour is treated.
pitfalls: Dismissing spontaneous (non-surgical) first bite pain and missing a parapharyngeal neoplasm
Confusing it with Frey syndrome, which causes sweating rather than pain
Attributing the mealtime pain to dental or temporomandibular disease
Failing to recognise the characteristic first-bite, sour-food pattern in the history
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
